rv.q: If the answer is not a triumphant yes – every actor in the new iteration is not ideal – then the answer is certainly, in a just-completed Broadway season without a knockout new musical, a very welcome yes.
The power of Mendes’s production comes from the confidence with which he allows the tawdry to teeter, and then fall so completely and brutally into the terrible.
This Cabaret is a superb production of one of the great Broadway musicals of all time—an exhilarating, harrowing masterpiece.
You’re left dazzled — and devastated.

Michelle Williams brings a bruised sensuality and surprising vocal authority to Sally Bowles in the latest Broadway revival of 'Cabaret,' turning in a performance that is both deeply felt and shrewdly calibrated.
Whatever it's called, it's as thrilling as ever, a marvel of staging that hasn't lost its punch.
In reality, the production, in toto, is the leading player here, including a wholly immersive Robert Brill design that manages not to feel like a set at all, until it is ready to reveal.
Cumming is better than ever -- wiser, more dissipated, even more deeply entertaining in the role he stunningly recreated from Joel Grey's iconic original.
Stone’s Sally loves the attention she got as “The Toast of Mayfair.”
It's so rare to get a second shot at seeing something this good, you should do anything you can to get a ticket.
She’s not the kind of girl you want to save but the kind you want to tiptoe away from, quietly, backwards.
It's a star turn that, even in this rich season, is truly unmissable — as is this Cabaret in general.
Shattering and utterly magnificent. Cabaret always promised to be the show of the season. It is that.

"Cabaret," which opened at Studio 54 Thursday night, is the last show of the 2013-14 Broadway season. And perhaps the most exciting. Yet, it's totally fresh and crisp, and completely seductive, with Alan Cumming repeating his memorable performance, and Hollywood's Michelle Williams making a triumphant Broadway debut.
Cumming is the master of this ceremony.
It's a show so smart, so daring, so substantial that it manages to be wildly entertaining about fascism and anti-Semitism.
“Cabaret” is a seductive piece of theater, beautifully designed and with stellar performances throughout.
Besides that final scene, Williams comes off paler and wispier than desired.
Cabaret continues to make beautiful music even though one of its principals falls rather flat.
This remounting is essentially that same show, which ran for almost six years.

Aside from Williams's serious misstep, the most noticeable drawback to the backward glance Mendes et al have made at this Cabaret is that the conviction, the sense of adventure, the challenge of doing it their way is lacking.

cn.t: This revival of the 1998 production earns praise for its dark, seductive staging and Alan Cumming's brilliant return as the Emcee, though some critics question restaging it so soon and find Michelle Williams credible but unmemorable.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
